tucson.intro: Tucson's oldest planted trees are a row of olives a professor put in on 1 April 1895, on the University of Arizona campus, as a trial of which varieties would grow here. The campus is a free outdoor arboretum, and a walk across it takes in a cork oak from before 1940, a sycamore grown from a seed that went to the Moon, a baobab and a calabash tree that fruits from its trunk. West of downtown, Phina's Tree, a river red gum, was called the city's largest tree by a 2009 sign.
tucson.meta_description: Tucson's old trees: the 1895 Olive Walk, a Moon tree, a baobab and a cork oak on the University of Arizona campus, and Phina's Tree on Congress Street.
tucson.question_meta: Tucson's oldest mapped trees are the Olive Walk on the University of Arizona campus, a row of olives planted on 1 April 1895.
tucson.question_answer: The oldest trees we map in Tucson are the olives of the Olive Walk on the University of Arizona campus, planted on 1 April 1895 by Robert Forbes, head of the Agricultural Experiment Station, which makes them more than 125 years old. Forbes gave the date himself in a 1934 talk, and the campus arboretum's records agree. The oldest single tree we can date with a sourced year is the African sumac between Maricopa and Yuma Halls, planted in 1928 from seed collected in South Africa in 1919.
tucson.question_context: Most of these trees stand on the University of Arizona campus, whose grounds are a designated arboretum and free to walk at any hour. Start at the Olive Walk, just north of Old Main, where gnarled olives line an east-west path for about 200 metres. Old Main is also where you find the date palm Iraqi students gave in 1955 in honour of Dean Eckert. South of the Engineering Building, a cork oak planted before 1940 stands a few steps from the campus's original floss silk tree, which flowers pink in October and November. Further east are the Moon tree sycamore by the Kuiper building, the calabash at the Main Library and the baobab at the Administration Building, both young but rare: the arboretum says the calabash is the only one of its size in Tucson. The live oak at the south end of the Park Avenue Green Belt is the largest of its kind in the city. Off campus, about three kilometres west on Congress Street, Phina's Tree, a river red gum, measured 95 feet tall on a 2009 city sign.

faq.q: Is the University of Arizona campus arboretum free?
faq.a: Yes. The trees stand on the open campus grounds, with no entry fee and no permission needed.

faq.q: What is the Olive Walk?
faq.a: A row of olive trees just north of Old Main, planted on 1 April 1895 as a variety trial by Robert Forbes. More than twelve cultivars survive in their original places.

faq.q: Is there a Moon tree in Tucson?
faq.a: Yes. A sycamore east of the Kuiper Sciences Building on the University of Arizona campus grew from a seed flown on Apollo 14 in 1971. A plaque from 1976 tells its story.

faq.q: Where is Phina's Tree?
faq.a: On the south side of West Congress Street, just west of the freeway and the Santa Cruz River, about three kilometres west of the campus. A 2009 city sign called it Tucson's largest tree.

boulder.intro: Boulder's old trees are almost all planted ones, and several are the biggest of their kind in Colorado. The City of Boulder's notable tree tour names the state's largest chestnut oak in Chautauqua Park, three of its largest sycamores beside a 1903 schoolhouse on Naropa University's campus, and its champion swamp white oak in Green Mountain Cemetery. On the University of Colorado campus, a yellow buckeye stands among the big trees around Hale Science, built in 1894.
boulder.meta_description: Boulder's old trees: Colorado's largest chestnut oak at Chautauqua, the champion swamp white oak in Green Mountain Cemetery, and century-old sycamores.
boulder.question_meta: Boulder's oldest mapped trees are three sycamores at Naropa University, planted soon after the Lincoln Elementary School opened in 1903.
boulder.question_answer: The oldest trees we map in Boulder are the three sycamores on Naropa University's Arapahoe Avenue campus. The City of Boulder says historic photographs show them planted not long after Lincoln Elementary School opened there in 1903, which makes them roughly 110 to 130 years old. Boulder's other old trees are dated the same way, from when their surroundings were laid out rather than from a planting record, so none of these ages is exact.
boulder.question_context: All five trees come from the City of Boulder's notable tree tour, published by its forestry team in 2021, and the newest record we have for each is that tour, so a recent photograph from a visitor is always welcome. Chautauqua Park, founded in 1898 and on the National Register of Historic Places, holds two of them about 30 metres apart: the chestnut oak the city calls the largest in Colorado and a white oak that turns red to maroon every October. Both are free to visit in a public park. The yellow buckeye stands near Hale Science on the open CU Boulder campus, a short walk from Pearl Street. Green Mountain Cemetery, established in 1905, holds the state champion swamp white oak, listed in Colorado's champion register at 42 inches across and 70 feet tall. The Naropa sycamores are on private university grounds; the city includes them on its public tour, but we have not found Naropa's own terms for visitors, so look from the edge of the grounds if unsure.

faq.q: Are Boulder's notable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Chautauqua Park and the CU Boulder campus are open and free. Green Mountain Cemetery is open to visitors, though we have not confirmed its hours.

faq.q: Where is the largest chestnut oak in Colorado?
faq.a: In Chautauqua Park, according to the City of Boulder, about 30 metres from a white oak on the same city tree tour.

faq.q: When do Boulder's trees show autumn colour?
faq.a: The Chautauqua white oak turns red to maroon reliably each October, according to the city's tree tour.

santa-fe.intro: Santa Fe's oldest tree that we map is a horse chestnut on Canyon Road, planted between about 1865 and 1880 and now well past the usual lifespan of its kind. On the Plaza, a massive elm shades the courtyard behind the Palace of the Governors, beside a cottonwood the king and queen of Spain planted in 1987. On the State Capitol grounds stands a Douglas-fir grown from a seed that orbited the Moon, lost for decades and identified again in 2019.
santa-fe.meta_description: Santa Fe's old trees: the El Zaguán horse chestnut on Canyon Road, the Palace courtyard elm, and the Moon tree on the State Capitol grounds.
santa-fe.question_meta: Santa Fe's oldest mapped tree is the horse chestnut in the El Zaguán garden on Canyon Road, planted around 1865 to 1880.
santa-fe.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Santa Fe is the horse chestnut in the El Zaguán garden at 545 Canyon Road, somewhere between 145 and 160 years old. The Historic Santa Fe Foundation, which owns the garden, says Maria Jesusita Johnson planted it with a partner tree around 1880; a 2013 newspaper report put the planting around the end of the Civil War. Its partner died in 2013.
santa-fe.question_context: All three trees are within walking distance of the Plaza. The horse chestnut is about 15 minutes east, on Canyon Road, in the garden of El Zaguán, a house the Historic Santa Fe Foundation keeps with shop and exhibit hours; the foundation does not publish garden hours or an entry fee, so check before you go. About half its roots run under the street, and drought has stressed it. It flowers in May. The Palace of the Governors courtyard is on the north side of the Plaza, two minutes away; the elm there is known to us only from a state museum photo caption, which calls it a Chinese elm more than 100 years old, and in New Mexico that name often means Siberian elm. Whether you need a museum ticket to reach the courtyard we have not confirmed. The Moon tree is about ten minutes south-west, on the open grounds of the Roundhouse. NASA says the tree identified in 2019 is believed to be the right one, and a recent visitor places it as the middle of three firs below a concrete balcony.

faq.q: Where is the Moon tree in Santa Fe?
faq.a: On the New Mexico State Capitol grounds, in a grassy area north of the Roundhouse. Its plaque disappeared, and the tree was identified again in 2019, so it is believed rather than proven to be the Moon tree.

faq.q: Can I visit the El Zaguán garden?
faq.a: The house at 545 Canyon Road keeps shop and exhibit hours. The Historic Santa Fe Foundation does not publish separate garden hours or a fee, so check with them before you go.

faq.q: When is the horse chestnut in flower?
faq.a: In May, when white flower candles stand upright over the crown.

prescott.intro: Prescott has two Arizona white oaks estimated at more than 300 years old, both within a few minutes' walk of the Courthouse Plaza. One, on Cortez Street, was recognised in 1976 as alive at the time of the American Revolution. The other stands in a library car park the city built around it. On the plaza itself, the Statehood Tree, a deodar cedar planted in 1910 or 1912 depending on whom you ask, doubles as the town's Christmas tree.
prescott.meta_description: Prescott's old trees: two Arizona white oaks over 300 years old near the Courthouse Plaza, and the Statehood Tree, planted in 1910 or 1912.
prescott.question_meta: Prescott's oldest mapped tree is the Bicentennial Tree on Cortez Street, an Arizona white oak a 1976 plate estimated at 340 years old.
prescott.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Prescott is the Bicentennial Tree, an Arizona white oak on Cortez Street. A brass plate added to its 1976 marker estimates it at 340 years old then; later press gives 300 or more than 350, so we put it at roughly 300 to 360. The oak by the public library is close behind, estimated by its marker at over 300 years. Neither age comes from a ring count.
prescott.question_context: All three trees are on foot from the Courthouse Plaza, the town's public square, and free to see. The Statehood Tree stands at the plaza's northeast corner on the Gurley Street side, beside a bronze plaque on a granite boulder placed by Cub Scouts in 1960. That plaque dates the planting to 14 February 1912, Arizona's statehood day, while the Sharlot Hall Museum, citing a 1910 newspaper, says the cedar was planted on 4 July 1910. The state lists it as a witness tree. The Bicentennial Tree is about three minutes south on Cortez Street, beside the old City Hall block, and stands behind protective fencing while that block is redeveloped, so you see it from the pavement. The library oak is about six minutes away, in a small park area in the southeast corner of the library car park, reached from South Alarcon Street. A marker there says the city bought the land in 1998 and laid out the lot to keep the tree.

faq.q: What is the Statehood Tree in Prescott?
faq.a: A deodar cedar at the northeast corner of the Courthouse Plaza, planted in 1910 or 1912; the plaque and the local museum disagree on the year. It is also the town's Christmas tree.

faq.q: Can I get close to the Bicentennial Tree?
faq.a: For now you see it from the pavement on Cortez Street. It stands behind protective fencing while the old City Hall block beside it is redeveloped.

faq.q: How old are Prescott's oak trees?
faq.a: Both are estimates rather than ring counts. The Cortez Street oak was put at 340 years old in 1976, and the library oak's marker says over 300.

scottsdale.intro: Scottsdale's oldest trees were planted by the man the town is named after. In 1896 Chaplain Winfield Scott set a row of olives around his citrus grove as a windbreak. The citrus is gone, but about 25 of the olives were still counted in 2010, along the Drinkwater Boulevard median and four on Second Street, in front of the Civic Center in Old Town. In 2011 they were named an Arizona Centennial Witness Tree.
scottsdale.meta_description: Winfield Scott's olives, planted in 1896 as a windbreak around his citrus grove, still stand at Second Street and Drinkwater Boulevard, Scottsdale.
scottsdale.question_meta: Scottsdale's oldest mapped trees are Winfield Scott's olives, planted in 1896 around his citrus grove in what is now Old Town.
scottsdale.question_answer: The oldest trees we map in Scottsdale are the olives Chaplain Winfield Scott, the town's founder, planted in 1896 as a windbreak around his citrus grove. That makes them about 130 years old. The Scottsdale Historical Society says a few still stand along Civic Center, and a 2025 article confirms they are still there.
scottsdale.question_context: The olives grow on public street medians in Old Town, free to see at any hour. A 2010 account counted about 25 survivors, most forming the median of Drinkwater Boulevard between Second Street and Osborn Road, with four still on Second Street near Drinkwater, in front of the Scottsdale Civic Center. The four on Second Street are the place to stand: they mark the edge of the grove Scott planted. When a hospital was built nearby, its ambulance entrance went in between two of the original trees. In 2011 the olives were named an Arizona Centennial Witness Tree, meaning they were already standing when Arizona became a state in 1912. Nobody has published measurements of their trunks, so we cannot tell you which one is the biggest. Scottsdale is about 30 to 45 minutes from downtown Phoenix by bus, and Old Town is easy to walk once you are there.

faq.q: Who planted the olive trees in Old Town Scottsdale?
faq.a: Chaplain Winfield Scott, the town's founder, in 1896, as a windbreak around his citrus grove.

faq.q: Where exactly are Winfield Scott's olives?
faq.a: Four stand on the Second Street median near Drinkwater Boulevard, in front of the Civic Center. More line the Drinkwater Boulevard median between Second Street and Osborn Road.

faq.q: Is it free to see them?
faq.a: Yes. They grow on public street medians and can be seen at any time.

glendale-arizona.intro: Glendale, Arizona, keeps some of the oldest date palms in the state at Sahuaro Ranch Park. In 1891 the ranch's second superintendent, Harry W. Adams, planted about twenty date seedlings beside the Main House to test whether dates could be grown commercially. The City of Glendale calls it one of the oldest date groves in Arizona. The ranch, with its 1886 Main House, is on the National Register of Historic Places and free to visit.
glendale-arizona.meta_description: Sahuaro Ranch's 1891 date palms in Glendale, Arizona, planted beside the Main House as an experiment, in a free historic park.
glendale-arizona.question_meta: Glendale's oldest mapped trees are the date palms by the Main House at Sahuaro Ranch, planted in 1891.
glendale-arizona.question_answer: The oldest trees we map in Glendale are the date palms close to the Main House at Sahuaro Ranch Park, planted in 1891 by the ranch's second superintendent, Harry W. Adams. That makes them about 135 years old. The city does not say how many of the original twenty survive or which palms they are.
glendale-arizona.question_context: Sahuaro Ranch Park is at 9802 North 59th Avenue, free and open from 6 a.m. to sunset daily, except during some special events. The historic ranch at its heart includes the Main House, built in 1886, and the whole ranch is on the National Register of Historic Places. The palms worth seeking out are the ones close to the Main House. Do not confuse them with the larger, orderly date grove east of the ranch houses: that was planted later by Richard W. Smith, who owned the ranch after 1927. The 1891 planting began as an experiment in commercial date growing, and the city still calls it one of the oldest date groves in Arizona. None of the old palms carries a label we know of, so you are looking at the oldest palms by the house rather than one named tree. If you know which of them are the 1891 survivors, tell us. From downtown Phoenix, Glendale is roughly 45 minutes to an hour by bus.

faq.q: Is Sahuaro Ranch Park free?
faq.a: Yes. It is open from 6 a.m. to sunset daily, and admission is free except during certain special events.

faq.q: Which date palms are the old ones?
faq.a: The ones close to the Main House. The large grove east of the ranch houses was planted after 1927 and is not the 1891 planting.

faq.q: Who planted the first date palms at Sahuaro Ranch?
faq.a: Harry W. Adams, the ranch's second superintendent, planted about twenty seedlings in 1891 to test commercial date growing.

albuquerque.intro: The oldest trees on the University of New Mexico campus were planted by its students. Around 1905, President William G. Tight led faculty and students into the Sandia Mountains to collect ponderosa pines, and planted them beside Hodgin Hall, the university's first building. Tight Grove still stands at the corner of Central Avenue and University Boulevard, around a Lobo sculpture, and is listed on the National Register together with the hall.
albuquerque.meta_description: Tight Grove at the University of New Mexico: ponderosa pines students carried from the Sandia Mountains around 1905, beside Hodgin Hall.
albuquerque.question_meta: Albuquerque's oldest mapped trees are Tight Grove at the University of New Mexico, planted between 1905 and 1908.
albuquerque.question_answer: The oldest trees we map in Albuquerque are those of Tight Grove, beside Hodgin Hall at the University of New Mexico, planted by President William G. Tight with faculty and students. A university history page gives 1905; the National Register nomination for Hodgin Hall gives 1908. Either way the grove is more than 115 years old, though nobody has said how many of its trees are originals.
albuquerque.question_context: Tight Grove is the patch of pines and grass around a Lobo sculpture on the southwest corner of the main campus, directly beside Hodgin Hall, the Pueblo Revival building at Central Avenue and University Boulevard. It is open campus ground, free and with no posted hours; the university's grounds are a state-designated arboretum. Buses along Central Avenue stop a few minutes' walk away. The two sources disagree on more than the year. The university history page speaks only of ponderosa pines collected in the Sandia Mountains, while the National Register nomination says Tight and the student body planted Rio Grande Valley cottonwoods as well as mountain ponderosa, and that the grove was later named in his honour. Treat the grove as one place to stand rather than one tree. Groves get replanted over a century, and we have not seen a record of which trunks are first-generation, so if you know, tell us.

faq.q: What is Tight Grove?
faq.a: A grove of pines and grass beside Hodgin Hall at the University of New Mexico, planted by President William G. Tight with faculty and students in 1905 or 1908, and named after him.

faq.q: Is Tight Grove open to visitors?
faq.a: Yes. It is on the open university campus at Central Avenue and University Boulevard, free and with no posted hours.

faq.q: What trees are in Tight Grove?
faq.a: Ponderosa pines collected in the Sandia Mountains, and according to the National Register nomination also Rio Grande Valley cottonwoods.

denver.intro: In City Park, Denver keeps an elm with a plaque saying it grew from a cutting of the tree at Shakespeare's grave in Stratford. Wikipedia dates the planting to 23 April 1916, three hundred years to the day after Shakespeare died, though that part of the article carries no source, and the Stratford lineage has never been proven. It stands in the southeast part of the park, near 17th Avenue and Colorado Boulevard, free to visit.
denver.meta_description: Denver's Shakespeare Elm in City Park, said by its plaque to come from the tree at Shakespeare's grave and dated to 1916.
denver.question_meta: Denver's oldest mapped tree is the Shakespeare Elm in City Park, dated to 23 April 1916.
denver.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Denver is the Shakespeare Elm in City Park, a little over 110 years old if the planting date of 23 April 1916 is right. That date comes from Wikipedia's history of the park, in a passage without a source. Its plaque says it grew from a cutting of the tree at Shakespeare's grave, a claim nobody has proved.
denver.question_context: City Park is a free public park, open at all times, and buses run along both Colorado Boulevard and 17th Avenue. The elm stands in the southeast part of the park, near the corner of 17th Avenue and Colorado Boulevard, though one walking guide also describes an approach from 14th and Colorado. Our pin is an estimate of that corner rather than a fix on the trunk, so look for the plaque on the trunk. It reads that the scion it was grown from was taken from the tree at Shakespeare's grave at Stratford-on-Avon. A local guide calls it the elm supposedly grown from a switch off the grave, which is the right amount of doubt. The species is often given as wych elm, but we have not seen that on a source we could check, so we call it an elm. If you find it, a photograph taken at the trunk would let us put the pin in the right place.

faq.q: Where is the Shakespeare Elm in Denver?
faq.a: In the southeast part of City Park, near 17th Avenue and Colorado Boulevard. Look for the plaque on the trunk.

faq.q: Did the Shakespeare Elm really come from Shakespeare's grave?
faq.a: That is what its plaque says. Nobody has proved it, and a local guide calls it a tree supposedly grown from a switch off the grave.

faq.q: Is City Park free?
faq.a: Yes. It is a public city park, open at all times.

flagstaff.intro: In front of Old Main at Northern Arizona University stands an American elm planted on 22 April 1931 from a sprig of the Washington Elm of Cambridge, Massachusetts, a gift from the local chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution. In 2012 it was named an Arizona Centennial Witness Tree, though it was planted nineteen years after statehood. It stands on the open campus lawn, about 1.5 kilometres from downtown Flagstaff.
flagstaff.meta_description: NAU's Washington Elm in Flagstaff, planted in 1931 from a sprig of the Cambridge Washington Elm, on the lawn in front of Old Main.
flagstaff.question_meta: Flagstaff's oldest mapped tree is the Washington Elm in front of Old Main at Northern Arizona University, planted in 1931.
flagstaff.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Flagstaff is the American elm in front of Old Main at Northern Arizona University, planted on 22 April 1931, which makes it about 95 years old. The Daughters of the American Revolution gave it as a sprig of the Washington Elm in Cambridge, Massachusetts. That lineage is the plaque's account; the Cambridge story itself has been called a legend.
flagstaff.question_context: The elm stands on the lawn in front of Old Main, on the open NAU campus, free to visit at any hour. It is about 1.5 kilometres south-east of downtown Flagstaff, roughly twenty minutes on foot from the Amtrak station, and Mountain Line buses stop on campus. Two plaques sit at its base. The older is from the Coconino Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, recording the 1931 gift to what was then the Arizona State Teachers College at Flagstaff. The newer, from 2012, names it an Arizona Centennial Witness Tree, alive from 1912 to 2012, wording that belongs to the centennial programme rather than to a tree planted in 1931. The Washington Elm it is said to descend from is the Cambridge tree under which George Washington is said to have taken command of the Continental Army. Around 2011 the university reported the elm sick with European elm scale, and the DAR chapter gave a thousand dollars toward its treatment. We have not seen a recent report on its health.

faq.q: Where is the Washington Elm at NAU?
faq.a: On the lawn in front of Old Main on the Northern Arizona University campus in Flagstaff, with two plaques at its base.

faq.q: Is the NAU elm really from the Washington Elm?
faq.a: That is what the DAR plaque says. The story that Washington took command under the Cambridge elm has itself been called a legend.

faq.q: Is it free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It stands on the open campus lawn, free at any hour.

sedona.intro: Seven miles north of Sedona in Oak Creek Canyon, Slide Rock State Park keeps the apple orchard Frank Pendley started in 1912. Apples were the Pendley family's cash crop, and the homestead became a state park in 1987. The orchard, nearly 300 trees by the park's count, is still tended, and in April the whole planting is in blossom. Not every tree dates from 1912; the age belongs to the orchard as a whole.
sedona.meta_description: The Pendley apple orchard at Slide Rock State Park, planted from 1912 on a homestead in Oak Creek Canyon, seven miles north of Sedona.
sedona.question_meta: Sedona's oldest mapped trees are the Pendley apple orchard at Slide Rock State Park, first planted in 1912.
sedona.question_answer: The oldest trees we map near Sedona are those of the Pendley apple orchard at Slide Rock State Park, in Oak Creek Canyon, where Frank Pendley made his first plantings in 1912. That makes the orchard more than a century old. The park does not say how many of today's nearly 300 trees are originals, so the age is the orchard's rather than any one tree's.
sedona.question_context: Slide Rock State Park is about seven miles north of Sedona on US 89A, and there is no public transport, so you drive. The park charges an entry fee and on busy days admits by vehicle, so check Arizona State Parks' page for the current fee and hours before you set out. In early November 2026 floods closed the road and the park, which is another reason to check. The orchard stands on the old Pendley homestead inside the park. Frank Pendley established his first plantings in 1912, apples became the family's cash crop, and the land became a state park in 1987. In 2007 Arizona State Parks took the orchard's care back into its own hands, and it is still tended as a working orchard. Treat it as one place to stand rather than a single tree: the trees vary in age, and no source says which are the 1912 originals. April is the time to see it at its best, when the orchard blossoms.

faq.q: Is there an entry fee for Slide Rock State Park?
faq.a: Yes. It is a paid state park, and on busy days entry is by vehicle. Check Arizona State Parks for the current fee and hours.

faq.q: How old is the Slide Rock apple orchard?
faq.a: Frank Pendley made his first plantings in 1912, so the orchard is more than a century old. Not every tree in it is original.

faq.q: Can I get to Slide Rock by public transport?
faq.a: No. It is a drive of about seven miles north of Sedona on US 89A.

faq.q: When does the orchard blossom?
faq.a: In April.
